readerTitle: Four choices that fix a homepage headline
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션: 독립 식당용 근무표 소프트웨어 회사의 홈페이지 헤드라인 고쳐 쓰기. 식당 간판 예시 포함. 모든 인물과 문구는 설명용.
insight: 좋은 헤드라인은 방문자가 해야 할 번역(기술 용어를 내 문제로 바꾸는 일)을 대신 해 준다. 네 가지 결정이 모두 같은 일을 한다.
misconception: 헤드라인은 기억에 남고 인상적이어야 한다. 기술과 기능을 앞세울수록 전문적으로 보인다.

sources.text: MKT-04 유닛의 개념 정리 (기능 vs 혜택, 명확성, 고객의 말, 행동 유도, 반론 대응)
모든 인물, 회사, 문구, 시간은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "minutes", "two minutes" 등 시간 표현은 가상 제품의 설정입니다. 실제 통계나 연구 수치는 사용하지 않았습니다.
MKT-04-08(소프트웨어 홈페이지 고쳐 쓰기)과 사례가 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요. 이 레슨은 식당 고객을 둔 소프트웨어 회사와 연속 결정 구조로 차별화했습니다.
테이크어웨이의 "Next" 예고 문구는 다음 유닛이 확정되면 구체적으로 바꾸세요.

cards.title: Four choices that fix a homepage headline
body: Dana runs a small software company. Its app helps independent restaurants plan staff shifts. Owners who try it tend to keep it.
The problem is the homepage. Most visitors leave within seconds. The headline at the top reads: *Next-generation AI-powered workforce optimization.*
You're helping Dana rewrite it. Four decisions, one story.

image.label: Restaurant owner squinting at a jargon-filled website on a phone
image.brief: 식당 주방 뒤편, 앞치마를 두른 사장이 휴대폰 속 웹사이트를 보며 고개를 갸웃함. 화면에는 "Next-generation AI-powered workforce optimization" 문구. 실제 로고나 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should the headline lead with?
body: Dana's team has three directions. Each one is true about the product. Which should carry the main line?

options.text: How it's built: *AI scheduling engine with real-time labor forecasting*
options.feedback: Accurate, but owners don't buy an engine. Each visitor has to translate it into their own problem, and most won't stop to try.

options.text: What the owner gets: *Your staff rota, done in minutes*
options.feedback: It names the result. You give up sounding impressive, and you must be able to back up the claim.

options.text: Who it's for: *Scheduling for independent restaurants*
options.feedback: The right people recognise themselves, but nothing says why they should care. Strong as support, weak as the main line.

cards.title: Say you chose the benefit. Whose words do you use?
body: Dana has notes from 20 short calls with current customers. The team also has a brainstorm document full of slogans. Where should the wording come from?

options.text: A phrase owners kept repeating in calls: *I lose my Sunday night to the rota*
options.feedback: Visitors recognise their problem in their own words. Digging through notes takes time, but a brainstorm rarely beats it.

options.text: The team's favourite slogan from the brainstorm
options.feedback: Fast, and the team will love it. But it reflects how the team talks, not how owners describe their week.

options.text: Language borrowed from the biggest competitor's site
options.feedback: Familiar and safe, but you'll sound like everyone else. Their words may not come from customers either.

cards.title: Say you used the customers' words. Two finalists remain.
body: Draft 2: *Get your Sunday night back. Build next week's rota in minutes.*
The team loves Draft 1. It's catchy. Which goes on the page?

options.text: Draft 1, because the pun stands out
options.feedback: It may earn a smile, but a visitor who skims can't tell what you sell. A smile doesn't stop them leaving.

options.text: Draft 2, because it says plainly what you get
options.feedback: Less memorable, but a busy owner gets it in one glance. On a page people skim, that matters more.

options.text: The pun as the headline, Draft 2 as the smaller line below
options.feedback: Better than the pun alone, since the smaller line carries the meaning. But many visitors read only the biggest line.

cards.title: Say you chose Draft 2. Now the button underneath.
body: In calls, owners raised one worry before trying: *I don't have time to set up another system.* What goes under the headline?

options.feedback: Low pressure, but vague. It asks for a click without saying what happens next.

options.text: A button that says *Start free trial*
options.feedback: A clear next step, but the setup worry goes unanswered, so hesitant owners still hesitate.

options.text: *Build your first rota free*, with a small line: *Import your staff list in two minutes. No card needed.*
options.feedback: It names the exact next step and answers the main worry where the doubt appears. Only promise two minutes if it's true.

cards.title: Every move cut the visitor's work.
body: Before: *Next-generation AI-powered workforce optimization.* After: *Get your Sunday night back. Build next week's rota in minutes.*
The old line made owners turn tech terms into their own problem. The new one does that for them. **The reader shouldn't have to decode a headline.**
A restaurant's window sign works the same way. *Lunch in 10 minutes, back to work on time* tells a passing office worker more than *Culinary excellence since 2009*.

image.label: Old and new headline side by side
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 비교 이미지. 왼쪽은 회색 톤의 "Next-generation AI-powered workforce optimization", 오른쪽은 밝은 톤의 "Get your Sunday night back. Build next week's rota in minutes."와 버튼 "Build your first rota free". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A better headline is still a guess.
body: Dana's new line is a best guess until real visitors see it. Test it against the old one, or show the page to five owners for five seconds and ask what the company does.

Two limits. The promise must be true: if setup really takes an hour, *minutes* will cost trust later. And words can't fix a product people don't need. If visitors understand the page and still leave, the problem may not be the headline.

cards.title: A good headline does the translating so the customer doesn't have to.
body: Each of your four decisions used one idea from this unit:
list: **Lead with the result:** features vs benefits
**Borrow the customer's words:** the customer's own words
**Plain over a pun:** clarity beats cleverness
**Name the next step and answer the worry:** calls to action and answering objections
cards.callout: **Try it today:** read your homepage headline or shop sign to someone outside your industry. Ask what you sell and why it would matter to them.
